blocks.text: 12.5.5 Terraform for the Optimization Stack

Lessons 12.5.2 and 12.5.3 created a bucket, a compute environment, a job queue, a job definition, a state machine and four roles, each with a boto3 call against moto. In AWS someone has to create them too, the same way in staging and in production, and change them later without breaking the runs already stored. Clicking through the console does not repeat, and a script of boto3 calls does not know what already exists. **Terraform** does both: you describe the resources you want in files, it compares them with what exists, shows you the difference as a **plan**, and makes only that change. This lesson reads the GridCap stack's Terraform and writes a check that refuses a plan which would destroy history. (GridCap is fictional; no number in it is real.)

**This lesson is read-along for its Terraform.** The course's runner has no Terraform and no network, and the course has no AWS account: the `.tf` files below were never planned or applied. The Python programs that read the policy and a plan did run, and their output is printed. No model is built or changed here.
Terraform Describes the Stack, plan Shows the Change, apply Makes It

Terraform's configuration language, HCL, describes each piece as a **resource** block: a type from a **provider** (here `hashicorp/aws`), a local name, and arguments. A resource can refer to another's attributes, `aws_s3_bucket.runs.arn`, and Terraform orders the work from those references. It records what it created in a **state** file, which maps each block to the real resource's id.
The working loop has three commands:

rows: compare the files with the state and the real resources; save the planned changes
the saved plan as JSON, for programs to read
make exactly the saved changes, nothing else

blocks.text: Terraform's documentation calls the saved plan file opaque, meant for `apply`, and says to treat it as sensitive. Applying the saved file, rather than planning again inside `apply`, means what was reviewed is what happens. The stack's files sit in `deploy/terraform/`: `variables.tf` for what changes per environment (bucket name, image, subnets), `main.tf` for the resources, `outputs.tf` for the names the API's configuration reads afterwards.
The Bucket Keeps History: Versioning, No Public Access, prevent_destroy
The bucket holds every snapshot and result (lesson 12.5.3). Three blocks protect it:

items: **`prevent_destroy`** makes Terraform fail any plan that would destroy the bucket, including a replacement (destroy, then create). Terraform's documentation notes the limit: delete the whole block from the files and the protection goes with it.

**Versioning** is its own resource in the AWS provider. Lesson 12.5.3 showed why it matters: an overwritten snapshot was still recoverable. The provider's documentation adds that destroying this resource suspends versioning on the bucket.
**The public access block** turns on all four of S3's Block Public Access settings. The provider defaults each to `false`; AWS recommends turning all four on. Planning data never needs a public URL.

blocks.text: The image registry gets the same treatment for a different reason:

With immutable tags, a tag pushed once can never point at another image. CI tags each image with its commit (lesson 12.5.6), so a job definition that names a tag always runs the same bytes, which is lesson 12.5.1's point about pinning, carried to the registry.
Batch and Step Functions Are Declared the Way the Programs Created Them
The Batch resources match the moto calls of lesson 12.5.2 field for field. The compute environment and the job definition:

`container_properties` is the same JSON the boto3 call sent, written with `jsonencode`; references replace the literal ARNs. `max_vcpus = 16` caps the whole environment: at 2 vCPUs a job, at most eight solves run at once, and the rest wait in the queue, the throttle lesson 12.4.2's thread pool provided on one machine. The state machine reads the definition file of lesson 12.5.2 itself, so the JSON the program inspected is the JSON that is deployed:
There is no database resource. The run index is the API's local SQLite file (lesson 12.5.3), and everything the cloud side keeps is in the bucket.
Each Role Gets Only What Its Part Needs
Four roles, one per part, each **assumed** by one AWS service (the `assume_role_policy` names it):

rows: pull the image, write logs (AWS's managed execution policy)
submit, describe and stop Batch jobs; invoke the failure function

blocks.text: The job role's policy is a file, rendered by Terraform's `templatefile` with the bucket's ARN:

The worker reads snapshots and writes results, so that is all it may do: no `DeleteObject`, no write under `snapshots/`, no other bucket. Lesson 12.5.4 showed that moto checks no permissions, so the policy is checked by reading it. `job_policy.py` renders the same file with Python's `string.Template` (which reads `${bucket_arn}` the way `templatefile` does) and asks a small model of IAM, Allow statements matched by action and resource with `*` as a wildcard, about five requests:

s3:GetObject     snapshots/sha256/730c8b40b1eb.json     allowed
s3:PutObject     results/730c8b40b1eb/run-0007.json     allowed
s3:PutObject     snapshots/sha256/730c8b40b1eb.json     denied
s3:DeleteObject  results/730c8b40b1eb/run-0007.json     denied
s3:GetObject     results/730c8b40b1eb/run-0006.json     denied

The worker can do its job and nothing that would rewrite history. The model is deliberately small: it knows no `Deny`, no conditions and no other kinds of policy, so it confirms what this file says, not everything AWS will decide. The Step Functions role takes the policy the Step Functions documentation gives for `submitJob.sync`; its Batch actions name `*` because, the documentation explains, job ids exist only at run time.
<!-- practice 1 -->
A Plan Is Data: Stop the Ones That Destroy History

`terraform show -json` turns a saved plan into JSON, documented in Terraform's "JSON output format". Each entry of `resource_changes` has the resource's address and a list of `actions`: `["no-op"]`, `["create"]`, `["read"]`, `["update"]`, `["delete"]`, or a replacement, `["delete", "create"]` (destroy first) or `["create", "delete"]` (create first). A program can read it before `apply` runs, and refuse. `plan_review.py` stops any plan that would delete a resource holding history: the bucket, its versioning, or the image registry.
KEEPS_HISTORY = {"aws_s3_bucket", "aws_s3_bucket_versioning", "aws_ecr_repository"}

def blocked(change: dict) -> bool:
    return change["type"] in KEEPS_HISTORY and "delete" in change["change"]["actions"]

The plan it reads, `deploy/terraform/sample-plan.json`, was written by hand in the documented shape; no Terraform ran. It holds one change of each kind: someone removed the versioning block (a destroy), renamed the compute environment (the provider says a new name forces a new resource, so a replacement), updated the Lambda code, and added a policy:

aws_ecr_repository.solver              no change
aws_lambda_function.record_failure     update in place
aws_iam_role_policy.record_failure     create
aws_batch_compute_environment.fargate  replace (destroy first)
aws_s3_bucket_versioning.runs          destroy  <- blocked
apply allowed: False | stopped by: ['aws_s3_bucket_versioning.runs']

`prevent_destroy` on the bucket would not have caught this: the bucket is not destroyed, only its versioning resource, whose block was deleted from the files. The plan check sees the plan, not the files, so it catches it. Replacing the compute environment passes: it holds no data, and queued jobs are the only thing to plan around. Lesson 12.5.6 runs this check in CI, between `plan` and `apply`.
<!-- practice 2 -->
Summary

items: **Terraform describes the stack; `plan` shows the change; `apply` makes it.** Apply the saved plan, so what was reviewed is what happens.
**The bucket keeps history:** versioning, all four public-access blocks, `prevent_destroy`; the registry's tags are immutable.
**Batch and Step Functions are declared the way the programs created them;** the state machine reads the same definition file. No database resource: the index is the API's SQLite file.
**Each role gets only what its part needs.** The job reads `snapshots/*` and writes `results/*`.
**A plan is data: stop the ones that destroy history.** `resource_changes[].change.actions`.

blocks.text: Reference

rows: create; change in place; destroy; read a data source
fail any plan that destroys or replaces this resource
the four Block Public Access settings (default `false`)
an ECR tag can never move
render a file; read a file; write JSON

Amazon S3, [Block Public Access](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/access-control-block-public-access.html); AWS Step Functions, [Run AWS Batch workloads](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/step-functions/latest/dg/connect-batch.html) (the `.sync` IAM policy); Amazon ECS, [Task IAM roles](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonECS/latest/developerguide/task-iam-roles.html).
Challenges

items: Give the worker permission to read the result of an earlier run of the same snapshot (to pass it as a solution hint, lesson 4.3.3). Write the narrowest statement you can, and the request your `allows` must still deny.
A colleague wants `force_destroy = true` on the bucket "to make teardown easier in staging". What does it change, and how would you allow it in staging only?
Extend the plan check to refuse a replacement of the state machine while executions are running. What does it need to know that the plan does not say?

blocks.text: Design Note: The Files Are the Review

With Terraform, a change to the stack is a change to text: it goes through a pull request, a reviewer reads the diff, CI prints the plan, and the check of this lesson refuses what no reviewer should have to catch by eye. The console and ad-hoc scripts skip all of that, and leave a stack nobody can rebuild. Terraform's state file is the price: it must be stored safely (it is kept out of the image by lesson 12.5.1's `.dockerignore`) and shared by everyone who applies.
The Full Programs

Each snippet above is part of a complete program, and each program printed the output the lesson shows. Open one to read it whole, change it, and run it again: Run starts the program on your copy of the code, so the course's own files never change.

**job_policy.py.** Renders the job role's policy from the Terraform file and asks five requests (*Each Role Gets Only What Its Part Needs*). *Try:* Change `s3:GetObject` to `s3:Get*` in the policy file. Predict which denied line changes.
**plan_review.py.** Reads the sample plan and blocks deletes of resources that hold history (*A Plan Is Data*). *Try:* Change the versioning change's actions to `["update"]`. Predict the last line.
